linkages: Individual-level information from education registers is combined with risky-health-behavior information from health registers for the entire Danish population
Children are linked to their mothers and fathers, whose labour-market and education characteristics are measured the year prior to childbirth
Women are linked to their cohabiting partner, whose exact birthdate gives the partner's relative age
Women are linked to their grade-8 school peers, from whom the peers' average age is computed

sample.universe: All Danish women born in the months November through February in the years between November 1981 and February 1992 (for the men's analysis, all Danish men born in the same months and years)
sample.unit_of_observation: woman (one observation per woman; a separate cross-sectional regression is run for each outcome and each age or grade horizon)
selection_rules: Born in the months November through February, i.e. a bandwidth of +/- two months around the January 1 school-entry cutoff
Only pupils attending public schools, private or independent schools or boarding schools are included
Only women who enroll in the 8th grade for the first time in July through September (the expected months)
Only women who have the expected age in the 8th grade
Information on the full sample of 89,496 women is available until age 25; from age 26 the sample decreases by dropping the youngest cohort for each additional age
The sample is smaller for chlamydia at ages 15-17 because the data are only available from 1999
In the peers' average age specification, 18 women with no peers are excluded
sample.period: Cohorts born November 1981 - February 1992; all outcomes available until and including 2017
sample.n_individuals: 89,496 women (and about 89,215 men in Appendix Table A.12)

construction_notes: Background characteristics are centered on the cutoff so that they are measured at the same age regardless of calendar birth year; birth year is likewise centered on the cutoff rather than entered as calendar year
Distance to the cutoff is measured in days, with a linear trend allowed to vary on either side of New Year; a quadratic control function is reported in Appendix Table A.9
Bandwidth is +/- two months around New Year; +/- 1 month, +/- 3 months and the MSE-optimal bandwidth of Calonico et al. (2014) are reported in Appendix Table A.8
Indicators for missing variables are included alongside the background characteristics

Relative age for grade is observed in the 8th grade and treated as equivalent to relative age at school start; school starting age takes two values around New Year, 6.6 and 7.6 (6.8 for November 1 births and 7.4 for February 28 births)
Abortions are induced abortions; 97 % of abortions in the data occur in the first trimester
Alcohol poisonings are alcohol-related hospital contacts; because only ages 15-30 are considered, 97 % of the contacts are alcohol poisonings rather than liver disease or withdrawal
Births are dated as the first child's birthdate minus 280 days, the approximate time of conception
Pregnancy combines births, abortions and miscarriages
Outcomes are measured both as a dummy for an event by a given age, as a count of events by a given age, as an indicator for an event at a given age, and by a given number of years after the 8th grade
The peers' average expected school starting age used as an instrument is ESSA = 7.6-(birthmonth-1)/12

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity: no parent defies the school starting age rule regardless of the child's birthdate, which allows the estimates to be read as local average treatment effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued to be unlikely a priori (a defier would be a parent who always applies for an exemption); no formal test

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable: parents do not choose which side of the January 1 cutoff a child is born on in a way that is related to the school starting decision.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histogram of births around New Year (Appendix Fig. A.3) shows an irregularity attributed to planned C-sections not being performed on holidays; donut regressions excluding +/- 1 and +/- 7 days around New Year (Appendix Table A.11)

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: being born January 1 or later shifts the probability of being young-for-grade.
key_assumptions.supported_by: First stage in Table 2: -0.27 (0.01), described as highly significant

key_assumptions.assumption: The control function for distance to the cutoff is correctly specified (a linear trend in days allowed to vary on either side) and the chosen bandwidth of +/- two months is appropriate.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Alternative bandwidths of +/- 1 and +/- 3 months and the MSE-optimal bandwidth (Appendix Table A.8); a second-order polynomial control function (Appendix Table A.9)

key_assumptions.assumption: Relative age for grade measured in the 8th grade is equivalent to relative age for grade at school start, because very few children repeat or skip a grade and this is unrelated to being born before or after New Year.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A.1 (fraction of girls repeating a grade) and Appendix Table A.2 (first stage across grades for the 1997 and 2000 cohorts)
